info.title: Configuring and managing software RAID via mdadm

topic.para: MD-RAID is the native Linux software RAID stack handled directly by the kernel's md module.

Multiple Devices RAID (MD-RAID) is Linux’s native, kernel-level software RAID framework, designed to combine multiple physical drives into a single redundant logical volume without relying on proprietary hardware controllers or BIOS-based FakeRAID. Operating directly within the Linux block layer, it supports RAID levels 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, and 10, with management handled primarily through the mdadm utility. It features automatic boot-time array assembly, live status tracking via /proc/mdstat , background parity scrubbing, online capacity expansion, and hot-swaps for failed drives. Because it is hardware-agnostic and fully portable across Linux installations, MD-RAID remains the industry standard for flexible, vendor-independent storage redundancy.
The following core utilities, daemons, and system interfaces provide the primary tools for configuring, monitoring, and maintaining Linux MD-RAID arrays:

listitem.para: mdadm: The main command-line utility used to create, assemble, build, manage, monitor, and repair pure Linux software RAID arrays (RAID 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 10).
mdmon: A background daemon bundled with mdadm that monitors arrays using external metadata formats.
raid6check: A diagnostic tool included with mdadm packages used to verify and repair parity consistency on RAID 6 sets.
/proc/mdstat: A virtual system file used to instantly check real-time status, synchronization progress, and health of active MD arrays.

sys/block/$DEV/md: By storing attributes like array_state, sync_action, and degraded in separate single-value files, /sys/block/$DEV/md enables scripts to read specific RAID metrics directly, eliminating the need to parse text.

section.title: Naming software RAID devices
section.para: Adopting a clear naming convention for software RAID arrays is essential for efficient system administration. Incorporating the array's purpose or RAID level directly into its name allows for quick volume identification and prevents costly mistakes during routine maintenance.

section.title: Default names
section.para: By default, software RAID devices have names following the pattern mdN, where N is a number. For example, they can be accessed as /dev/md127 and are listed as md127 in /proc/mdstat and /proc/partitions.

section.title: Providing non-default names
section.para: As working with the default names might be clumsy, there are two ways how to work around this:

varlistentry.term: Providing a named link to the device

listitem.para: You can optionally specify a name for the RAID device when creating it with &yast; or on the command line with mdadm --create '/dev/md/ NAME'. The device name will still be mdN, but the link /dev/md/NAME will be created:
The device will still be listed as md127 under /proc.
If a named link to the device is not sufficient for your setup, add the line CREATE names=yes to /etc/mdadm.conf by running the following command:

This will cause names like myRAID to be used as a real device name. The device will not only be accessible at /dev/myRAID, but also listed as myRAID under /proc. Note that this will only apply to RAIDs configured after the change to the configuration file. Active RAIDs will continue to use the mdN names until they get stopped and reassembled.

warning.title: Incompatible tools
warning.para: Not all tools may support named RAID devices. If a tool expects a RAID device to be named mdN, it will fail to identify the devices.

section.title: Configuring software RAID for the root partition
section.para: Setting up a software RAID 1 array for the root partition in &productname; 16 via the command line requires strict adherence to execution order. Executing these steps out of order will result in an unbootable system or data loss.

This procedure configures a software RAID 1 root partition on a &productname; 16 UEFI system and assumes two identical raw disks, /dev/sda and /dev/sdb , using a GPT partition scheme with a small BIOS Boot Partition (EF02) to allow GRUB2 embedding without requiring UEFI.

itemizedlist.title: Prerequisites for using a software RAID device for the root partition

listitem.para: You need two hard disks to create the RAID 1 mirror device. The hard disks should be similarly sized. The RAID assumes the size of the smaller drive. The block storage devices can be any combination of local (in or directly attached to the machine), Fibre Channel storage subsystems, or iSCSI storage subsystems.

A separate /boot is generally not required for standard installations, as the boot loader can reside directly on the primary system drive. However, modern UEFI systems require an ESP (EFI System Partition) to hold boot files. A standalone /boot partition is only necessary under specific storage configurations, such as full-disk encryption, complex software RAID, or file systems unsupported by the boot loader.

For UEFI machines, you need to set up a dedicated /boot/efi partition. It needs to be VFAT-formatted, and may reside on the RAID 1 device to prevent booting problems in case the physical disk with /boot/efi fails.
If you are using hardware RAID devices, do not attempt to run software RAIDs on top of it.
If you are using iSCSI target devices, you need to enable the iSCSI initiator support before you create the RAID device.

If your storage subsystem provides multiple I/O paths between the server and its directly attached local devices, Fibre Channel devices, or iSCSI devices that you want to use in the software RAID, you need to enable the multipath support before you create the RAID device.

section.title: Resizing software RAID arrays with mdadm
section.para: This section describes how to increase or reduce the size of a software RAID 1, 4, 5, or 6 device with the Multiple Device Administration (mdadm(8)) tool.

Resizing an existing software RAID device involves increasing or decreasing the space contributed by each component partition. The file system that resides on the RAID must also be able to be resized to take advantage of the changes in available space on the device. In &productname;, file system resizing utilities are available for file systems Btrfs, Ext2, Ext3, Ext4, and XFS (increase size only).

The mdadm tool supports resizing only for software RAID levels 1, 4, 5, and 6. These RAID levels provide disk fault tolerance so that one component partition can be removed at a time for resizing. In principle, it is possible to perform a hot resize for RAID partitions, but you must take extra care for your data when doing so.

warning.title: Back up your data before resizing
warning.para: Resizing any partition or file system involves some risks that can potentially result in losing data. To avoid data loss, ensure that you back up your data before you begin any resizing task.

section.para: Resizing the RAID involves the following tasks. The order in which these tasks are performed depends on whether you are increasing or decreasing its size.

table.title: Tasks involved in resizing a RAID

entry.para: Resize each of the component partitions.
Increase or decrease the active size of each component partition. You remove only one component partition at a time, modify its size, then return it to the RAID.
The RAID does not automatically know about the increases or decreases you make to the underlying component partitions. You must inform it about the new size.
You must resize the file system that resides on the RAID. This is possible only for file systems that provide tools for resizing.

section.title: Increasing the size of a software RAID
section.para: Increasing the size of a software RAID involves the following tasks in the given order: increase the size of all partitions the RAID consists of, increase the size of the RAID itself and, finally, increase the size of the file system.

warning.title: Potential data loss
warning.para: If a RAID does not have disk fault tolerance, or it is simply not consistent, data loss results if you remove any of its partitions. Be very careful when removing partitions, and ensure that you have a backup of your data available.

section.title: Increasing the size of component partitions
section.para: Apply the procedure in this section to increase the size of a RAID 1, 4, 5, or 6. For each component partition in the RAID, remove the partition from the RAID, modify its size, return it to the RAID, then wait until the RAID stabilizes to continue. While a partition is removed, the RAID operates in degraded mode and has no or reduced disk fault tolerance. Even for RAIDs that can tolerate multiple concurrent disk failures, do not remove more than one component partition at a time. To increase the size of the component partitions for the RAID, proceed as follows:

Increase the size of the partition (/dev/sda2) by doing one of the following:

listitem.para: Increase the size of the partition, using a disk partitioner such as the &yast; Partitioner or the command line tool parted. This option is the usual choice.

Replace the disk on which the partition resides with a higher-capacity device. This option is possible only if no other file systems on the original disk are accessed by the system. When the replacement device is added back into the RAID, it takes much longer to synchronize the data because all of the data that was on the original device must be rebuilt.

If you get a message that tells you that the kernel could not re-read the partition table for the RAID, you must reboot the computer after all partitions have been resized to force an update of the partition table.

section.para: Alternatively, if you are replacing the disks and can install the new disks temporarily alongside the existing array, you can hot-replace the partitions. This will keep them in service until a new partition has been rebuilt as a spare, so the array does not enter a degraded state and remains fault-tolerant during the process. section.title: Increasing the size of the file system
section.para: After you increase the size of the array, you are ready to resize the file system.

You can increase the size of the file system to the maximum space available or specify an exact size. When specifying an exact size for the file system, ensure that the new size satisfies the following conditions:

listitem.para: The new size must be greater than the size of the existing data; otherwise, data loss occurs.
The new size must be equal to or less than the current RAID size because the file system size cannot extend beyond the space available.

note.para: Decreasing the size of a live RAID array is discouraged.

section.title: Monitoring software RAID devices
section.para: On modern systems, software RAID array monitoring is enabled by default via systemd integration and operates through the standard mdcheck services and timers (mdcheck_start.timer and mdcheck_continue.timer). These systemd units periodically invoke mdadm to perform background parity checks and detect drive degradation or failure.
Customizations of monitoring delays, mail notification recipients, and check intervals should be configured in /etc/sysconfig/mdadm.
